title: Unnecessary move animation in nested <transition-group>

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the reported scenario and pass all six independent tests, so the decision rests on how each handles the root cause and the adjacent cases the issue implies.

Root cause: an inner group measures its children in viewport coordinates, so the outer item's FLIP movement is counted as movement of the inner items and animated twice. Patch B subtracts exactly that: at render it samples the enclosing group item's position alongside the children's old positions, and in `updated` it subtracts the item's shift only when the nearest enclosing group is pending and `willMove()` confirms it will actually animate that movement. Sampling the origin and children in the same frame keeps the arithmetic consistent regardless of whether the inner group updates via the outer patch (child `updated` fires first) or via its own job (outer has already moved in the DOM); the `item.contains(root)` guard handles teleport/relocation. If the outer group has no move transition or does not update at all, the inner group still animates the full movement as it does today.

Patch A instead always measures relative to the nearest ancestor flagged as a group child. This is simple and correct for the issue's case, but it over-corrects: whenever a containing item moves without the outer group animating it (outer group lacks a `-move` transition, or the outer group does not re-render and the item is pushed by layout, e.g. a bottom-anchored stack growing), inner children now silently lose the move animation they had on base. That is a behavioural regression in plausible nested setups, and it is baked into the design rather than being an oversight. The marker also persists on elements and is only set after the outer group's first re-render, which is fine in practice but adds a subtle ordering dependency.

Tests: A adds jsdom unit tests with a mocked `getBoundingClientRect` layout plus one e2e test; they would fail before and pass after for the headline case, but they only assert class presence. B adds a larger e2e suite with exact pre/post-click `top` values and classes covering outer-only move, outer without move transition, growth pushing a sibling, inner updating via its own job, three levels with and without a moving middle group, a moving outer item with no outer update, and teleport across the item. Several of these would expose A's regression, and they are tied directly to the behaviour under test rather than being tautological.

Scope/craft: B is considerably larger and more intricate (lazy `willMove`, `pendingGroups` WeakMap, `Origin` records), which carries real risk, and the extra `hasCSSTransform` probe from a child group adds a DOM write/read outside the usual loop. But the added machinery is what makes the fix precise rather than unrelated churn, it is well commented, and the WeakMap keying avoids leaks. A is cleaner in line count and consistent with the existing symbol-keyed element properties, but its correctness gap outweighs its brevity under the stated priority order. B wins on correctness and test strength.

### Version
3.2.30

### Reproduction link
[github.com](https://github.com/scx567888/error-example)







### Steps to reproduce
npm run dev 
en :  and click green or red button to change sort
中文 : 然后点击绿色或红色的按钮调整列表顺序


### What is expected?
en : Only the outermost div has transition animation
中文 : 只有最外层的 div 有过渡动画

### What is actually happening?
en : Inner div also has transition animation
中文 : 内部的 div 同样产生了过渡效果

---
en : i find add a css can fix this bug
中文 : 我发现添加一个 css 可以修复这个 bug

.scx-group-list-move .scx-group-list-move {
    transition: unset;
}

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the issue's root cause the same way: the leaving hooks that BaseTransition sets on the component vnode are now propagated through the dev root Fragment to the actual root element (and through a nested component), so the element performs the leave and calls afterLeave, which unsticks out-in mode. The independent tests pass identically on both. The differences are in robustness and completeness.

Patch A rewrites the Fragment branch of `remove` so a transition-carrying fragment leaves through its real root (`getTransitionRoot`) and is then removed as a whole range via `removeFragment`. This also fixes a defect that Patch B inherits from the existing dev-only path: that path removes only the fragment's children and never removes the fragment's own start/end text anchors, so every toggle leaks two empty text nodes. B's tests cannot see this because `serializeInner` hides empty text nodes; A's tests explicitly assert `root.children` length returns to 1 and the e2e test asserts `childNodes.length`. A is also not gated on `__DEV__`, so a build compiled with `comments: true` in production (where the compiler emits the same fragment without the DEV_ROOT_FRAGMENT flag) is fixed too; B's fix is dev-only by construction. A further handles edges B leaves broken: same-key re-entry while a comment-root component is still leaving (looks up the leave callback on the real root instead of the fragment anchor), an ancestor removing the fragment mid-leave (guards `removeFragment` on a detached node, which would otherwise throw on `nextSibling` of null), and multi-root fragments no longer getting stuck in out-in because the guard uses `getTransitionRoot` returning undefined.

B is smaller and mirrors existing dev-fragment conventions, and it adds a sensible renderComponentRoot change so a fragment unmounted outside BaseTransition (its Suspense test) still animates, which A does not cover. But B's unit tests use hand-built vnodes rather than compiled templates, only dev mode, no e2e, and do not check node counts, so they miss the anchor leak.

Scope-wise A's change to prod `remove`/`setTransitionHooks` is broader, but it is parametrized over `__DEV__` true/false, out-in/in-out, KeepAlive, element/component/nested roots, plus e2e class assertions and an integration test, which mitigates the risk. On correctness and test strength A is clearly ahead; B's advantages (minimality, Suspense case) do not outweigh leaving the anchor leak and the production path unaddressed.

title: watch callback has something side effect when calling `createApp` in the callback

judge.reasoning: Both patches target the real root cause: the root `render()` path flushes the global pre-job queue, so an `app.mount()` inside a pre watcher runs sibling watchers nested inside the current callback. Both filter the flush to jobs with `id >= nextUid` (components the mount actually created), and the independent tests confirm both restore the 1,2,1,2 order. Patch B is a tight, low-risk change: it only applies the filter when `flushIndex >= 0` (i.e. inside a running job) and appends an optional parameter, leaving everything else as-is. However it still calls `flushPostFlushCbs()` unfiltered, so a mount inside a pre watcher still runs every pending post cb (post watchers, mounted/updated hooks of other components) nested inside the callback and before the pending component re-renders, which is the same class of side effect the issue reports; it also inherits the base bug where `isFlushing` is never reset if a flushed job throws. Patch A applies the ownership rule uniformly: a mount/unmount flushes only the pre jobs of components it created and only the post cbs it queued (snapshot set plus owner tagging on watcher jobs), wraps the flush in try/finally, handles the compat case where the root instance exists before `$mount` (using `vnode.component.uid` rather than `getNextUid()`, which B would get wrong in compat inside a job), and leaves component-less watchers to the scheduler. Its tests are substantially more thorough and would fail on base (nested mount in pre watcher, post-watcher sibling order, mount in post watcher, compat `$mount`, root-update rescan). The cost is a much larger and more invasive change: a new `flushOnAppMount` abstraction, a middle-position signature change to `flushPreFlushCbs`, a restart-from-`flushIndex` rescan loop, a tri-state `job.i` (undefined/null/instance) encoding, and a change to unmount so it flushes no pre jobs (harmless since stopped effects are no-ops, but a behaviour change). That added surface is a real risk and B's minimalism is attractive, but on the primary criterion A resolves the reported side effect more completely (pre and post) and fixes the error-handling edge, and its tests pin the behaviour down far better. A wins on correctness and tests; B wins only on scope/risk.

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the independent reproduction tests pass, so the decision rests on root cause versus workaround and on risk.

The reporter's diagnosis is that the queued `mounted` hooks run after a same-flush `beforeUpdate`, so the stale initial binding is restored into the input. Patch A fixes that ordering: it records the post-flush callbacks queued by a component's mount (`startMount`/`endMount`), and when that component updates later in the same flush it runs those pending mounted hooks, refs and subtree hooks first (`flushPendingMountCbs`), with a `WeakMap` so an element mounted during a parent's update and patched again in the same flush also gets `mounted` before `beforeUpdate`. The resulting order (`mounted:bug`, `beforeUpdate:ok`, `updated:ok`) matches the documented lifecycle, and it also corrects component `onMounted` and template refs, which suffer from the same ordering defect. The uid-based filter that keeps post watchers of earlier components out of the early run is a heuristic, but it is commented and tested, and I could not construct a scenario where it runs a callback for a non-descendant.

Patch B keeps the wrong order and instead rewires `invokeDirectiveHook` so a pending `mounted` is invoked with the latest vnode's bindings (`_mount`/`_latest` chain on vnodes, with a copied binding to reset `oldValue`). Its own tests codify `beforeUpdate 1 0` running before `mounted 1 undefined 1`, so a directive that initializes state in `mounted` and relies on it in `beforeUpdate` stays broken, and `mounted` now receives a vnode other than the one that was mounted with `prevVNode` null. It is a tidy, localized workaround and it also handles the Suspense-deferred variant that A deliberately skips, but that variant is outside the issue's scenarios, and the fix addresses the symptom (value) rather than the cause (order) named in the issue title.

On tests, both add meaningful, non-tautological tests that fail on base; A covers the directive, component lifecycle, element-patched-during-update and post-watcher-isolation paths plus v-model; B covers v-model text/checkbox, Suspense and inherited directives. On scope, A is a larger scheduler change that touches hot paths (an extra array push per post cb during a flush, a WeakMap lookup per patchElement, a Map lookup per component update), which is real added risk, but it is contained to the same-flush mount-then-update case and cleared at flush end. Weighing root-cause correctness first, A is the better fix despite its larger footprint.

The core of the issue is incorrect queued hooks execution order, and most changes you would do to the repro are going to fix it.
If you want to see the page working correctly from the get go, just remove the timeout in `App.vue` and directly set `page.value = Page`.

Here's what I found out when debugging this myself:

The input is driven by a `v-model`, so the value is not really "rendered" by script setup, but it's instead set on elements by `vModelText` core directive. This will explain why the interpolation `{{ val }}` is rendered with the correct value, whereas the `<input>` shows the initial value instead.

The reproduction is setup in such a way that `vModelText` hooks are called in incorrect order.
After event `onSetup` is processed by `Wrapper`, the component is rendered again, and `vModelText.beforeUpdate` is called with the new value. If you break at this point you'll see the repro displaying the correct values.

But then, it looks like the directive `mounted` hook has not been executed yet. It is enqueued by Vue core `mountElement` function here: 
https://github.com/vuejs/core/blob/fc4bbf95c1f9c8d9591e82571008578da15d7677/packages/runtime-core/src/renderer.ts#L715-L725

The issue seems to be that this call has captured the initial directive value and so restores the previous, incorrect value into the input element.

title: Iterating a reactive array makes spread, Array.from(array) and new Float32Array(array) 10–80× slower for the whole page

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the same way at its core: stop adding an own `next` to a native array iterator and return a wrapper instead. The independent protector tests confirm both restore the fast path for for...of, values()/entries(), and readonly arrays. The difference is in correctness at the edges the surrounding code already supports (the existing `extend methods` test shows user-extended Array subclasses are a supported scenario).

Patch A unconditionally wraps whatever `arr[method]()` returns, using `Object.create(getPrototypeOf(getPrototypeOf(iter)))`. For a native array iterator that yields %IteratorPrototype%, which works but drops the `Array Iterator` toStringTag. For a subclass whose iterator is a generator, the grandparent prototype is %GeneratorPrototype%, so the wrapper inherits `return`/`throw` that require a generator receiver; a `for...of` with `break` then calls `wrapped.return()` and throws a TypeError. Any custom iterator's `return`/`throw` are also silently lost, which the old code preserved (it returned the original iterator). So A fixes the perf bug but introduces a functional regression for extended arrays with custom iterators.

Patch B only wraps when the result is actually a native array iterator (toStringTag check, which also covers cross-realm), inherits from the native array iterator prototype so toStringTag, Symbol.iterator and iterator helpers keep working, and forwards `return`/`throw` lazily to the native iterator when a custom method produced it. Non-native iterators keep the original patching, which does not touch the protector. The `Object.create` wrapper is a plain object, not a JSArrayIterator, so it cannot trip the protector; B's own test asserts this and the independent tests agree.

Tests: both add a protector check that fails before and passes after. B additionally covers early-exit closing of generator and native iterators, iterator helper value wrapping for reactive/readonly/subclass arrays, and lazy return/throw forwarding, i.e. exactly the regressions A would introduce. A's structural 'no own keys below ArrayIteratorProto' test is useful but weaker.

Scope: B's extra code is justified because it guards against a regression the wrapper approach otherwise causes; it is not unrelated churn. Craft is comparable; B leaves a stale `_next` in the type cast but that is cosmetic. B is the better fix.

### Vue version

3.5.43

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

Open the playground link (or run the snippet) and compare the two columns. The arrays being spread and converted are plain, non-reactive arrays.

### What is expected?

Operations on plain arrays run at the same speed after a reactive array has been iterated.


### What is actually happening?

From the playground, Vue 3.5.43, Chrome 153, macOS, tab visible (median of 21 timings, ms):

| operation | before | after one `for…of` over `reactive([{}])` |
|---|---|---|
| `[...arr]` × 450 (1000 items) | 0.10 | 8.00 |
| `f(...arr)` × 450 | 0.90 | 8.40 |
| `Array.from(arr)` × 450 | 0.10 | 6.20 |
| `new Float32Array(arr)` (450k items, incl. building the array) | 1.50 | 15.40 |

Not affected in our measurements: `for…of`, `f.apply(null, arr)`, `Array.from({ length }, fn)`, `push`, `map`/`filter`/`slice`/`concat`.

Importing Vue alone changes nothing; the first iteration of a deep-reactive array does, and it lasts for the life of the V8 isolate (in Chrome, the renderer process, so same-site pages sharing that process are affected too). In a Nuxt 4 app it's triggered during startup (by the `@nuxt/icon` and `@nuxtjs/supabase` plugins iterating reactive arrays), so every page is affected, in dev and production. For us it makes a three.js layout step about 20% slower than the same code where the fast path is intact.

### System Info

```shell
Chrome 153.0 (macOS), Vue 3.5.43, Nuxt 4.5, macOS Version 26.6.2 (25G83)
```

### Any additional comments?

### Cause

`iterator()` in `packages/reactivity/src/arrayInstrumentations.ts` (used by `[Symbol.iterator]`, `values` and `entries` on reactive arrays) adds an own `next` property to the native array iterator:

```js
iter._next = iter.next
iter.next = () => { … }
```

V8 treats an own `next` on an array iterator as a change to array iteration and permanently invalidates its "array iterator" protector. After that, spread, `Array.from` of iterables and typed-array construction from arrays take the generic, much slower path.

### Possible fix

Return a wrapper iterator instead of mutating the native one. Inheriting from `%IteratorPrototype%` keeps `[Symbol.iterator]` and the iterator helpers:

```js
function iterator(self, method, wrapValue) {
  const arr = shallowReadArray(self)
  const iter = arr[method]()
  if (arr !== self && !isShallow(self)) {
    const wrapped = Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.getPrototypeOf(iter)))
    wrapped.next = () => {
      const result = iter.next()
      if (!result.done) {
        result.value = wrapValue(result.value)
      }
      return result
    }
    return wrapped
  }
  return iter
}
```

Served in place of the original in our app, this kept spread at 0.2 ms and typed-array construction at its normal speed, and the app behaved the same (its computed readouts were identical). We haven't run Vue's own test suite against it.

title: Errors thrown in async setup are caught silently during SSR

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the issue names: the `.catch(NOOP)` that wrapped the whole setup promise is narrowed so it only swallows onServerPrefetch failures, and both also handle a synchronous throw from a prefetch call (A via `Promise.resolve().then(...)`, B via try/catch). All six independent tests pass on both, and both add tests that fail on base and cover the key regressions (async setup with/without render function, prefetch registered then throw, sync prefetch error still rendering, errorCaptured for prefetch errors in A).

The meaningful difference is what happens once setup errors actually propagate. renderComponentVNode's promise is pushed into the SSR buffer and only awaited by unrollBuffer in order. With Patch A, if an earlier sibling is still pending (e.g. a real I/O fetch) when a later component's setup rejects, that rejection is unhandled for at least one tick, which Node reports as an unhandled rejection and, under the default `--unhandled-rejections=throw`, crashes the process. The issue's scenario (async setup throwing during SSR) makes this a realistic consequence of the fix, not a hypothetical. Patch B anticipates it with `p.catch(NOOP); return p`, which marks the rejection as observed while still returning the rejecting promise to the caller, and it adds tests ('while awaiting an earlier sibling' with setImmediate) that would surface the unhandled rejection under Patch A. B also makes renderToString/renderToStream stop registered watchers and settle in-flight buffer promises on a failed render, which is defensible cleanup now that renders can reject, though it is beyond the ask.

On scope, B is considerably broader (new cleanupFailedRender/settleBuffer helpers, stream error path change, test helper change to reject with the error). That breadth adds some risk and a reviewer could reasonably prefer A's minimal diff, but the core fix in B is equally correct and the extra code is cohesive and tested. A is the cleaner minimal patch and its tests are well targeted, but it leaves a real process-crash hazard that B's fix handles, so B is the better fix overall.

### Vue version

3.5.43

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://stackblitz.com/edit/vitejs-vite-kyxtdywv?file=main.js

### Steps to reproduce

Open the reproduction link, which performs the following steps:

1. Throws an error from a component's async setup.
2. Renders the component using `renderToString`.

### What is expected?

The error should propagate up to the `renderToString` call, causing it to return a rejected promise.

In the minimal reproduction, that rejection would be uncaught, so the error would appear in the Node.js console.

### What is actually happening?

There's no uncaught error or unhandled promise rejection. The console only displays the following warnings:

```
[Vue warn]: Unhandled error during execution of setup function 
  at <App>
[Vue warn]: Component App is missing template or render function. 
  at <App>
```

Also, if there is a render function in the component throwing the error, it renders successfully as if no error occurred.

### Any additional comments?

This bug is caused by https://github.com/vuejs/core/commit/349eb0f0ad78f9cb491278eb4c7f9fe0c2e78b79#diff-96591cb7eb061552355cc70e508472b1acc2688c3449ad0daa19c3cbac08cc97R100, where `onServerPrefetch` was added. Originally, the bug only occurred when the setup synchronously calls `onServerPrefetch`.

That line intended to catch errors thrown from `onServerPrefetch` callbacks, but the `.catch` was mistakenly applied to the entire setup promise.

The bug was expanded to occur in all async setups in https://github.com/vuejs/core/commit/6039e25e04a8c1db5821955f011d57f1615807ab#diff-96591cb7eb061552355cc70e508472b1acc2688c3449ad0daa19c3cbac08cc97R110 by no longer gating the `.catch` behind `if (prefetches)`.

title: KeepAlive deactivates its current child instead of unmounting it when unmounted after re-rendering under a pending ancestor Suspense (instance leaks)

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the four independent tests pass, so both fix the exact reported scenario (same-root re-render of the KeepAlive'd Suspense while the ancestor is pending, then unmount). The difference is where and how broadly they intervene.

Patch A fixes the invariant that actually breaks in KeepAlive's onBeforeUnmount: when the subTree is a Suspense whose patch was skipped, the mounted vnode is `suspense.activeBranch`, not `ssContent`, so it resets the flag on the active branch and also on the cached entry (the same approach #15711 already uses in pruneCacheEntry, and the exact fix the reporter validated). When the inner Suspense is in a normal state activeBranch === ssContent, so there is no behaviour change outside the broken case. Its four tests cover the issue scenario, a second non-visible cached child, and switching the KeepAlive child (new or cached) while the ancestor is pending; tracing the 'cached' variant shows A correctly unmounts both Tab (active branch) and Other (storage container), whereas the unchanged KeepAlive code under B would pick the never-activated `Other` ssContent as 'current', re-queue a deactivated hook on it, and leave it in the storage container.

Patch B rewrites the Suspense early-return so a nested boundary in retained (on-screen) content is patched while the parent is pending, except for root replacements. This does address the underlying skip the issue traced, and it is thoughtfully done (suspenseId-based 'retained' detection, deps-without-pendingBranch handling, a #8678 regression test). But it is a semantic change in a region with a documented history of regressions (#8678 → #10055 → #10184): retained content now visibly re-renders while the parent is pending (its own test asserts `tab 1`), which the issue did not ask for and which widens the blast radius. It also deliberately keeps the skip for root replacements, so the same KeepAlive flag-reset bug persists for the child-switch-while-pending variants, because KeepAlive's onBeforeUnmount is left assuming `getInnerChild(subTree)` is the mounted vnode.

On correctness for the reported issue both hold; on robustness across the issue's related KeepAlive cases A covers more; on scope and risk A is the narrower, lower-risk change consistent with existing conventions, while B's extra work adds risk rather than earning credit. A wins.

### Vue version

3.5.44 (also 3.6.0-rc.11, and `main` in the SFC playground)

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

The reproduction runs by itself on mount, just open it and read the log. The tree is:

```
<Suspense>                     <!-- root boundary -->
  <Shell v-if="page === 'shell'">
    <KeepAlive>
      <Suspense>
        <Tab :count="count" />
      </Suspense>
    </KeepAlive>
  </Shell>
  <NextPage v-else />          <!-- async setup, resolves after 100ms -->
</Suspense>
```

1. Switch the root `<Suspense>` from `Shell` to `NextPage`. `NextPage` has an async setup, so the root boundary goes pending and keeps `Shell` mounted.
2. While it is pending, change `count`, so the `<KeepAlive>` inside `Shell` re-renders.
3. Let `NextPage` resolve. The root boundary unmounts `Shell`.

### What is expected?

`Tab` is unmounted together with `Shell` and its `<KeepAlive>`: the log shows `Tab deactivated` and then `Tab unmounted`, the same as without step 2.

### What is actually happening?

The log shows `Tab deactivated` twice and never `Tab unmounted`. `Tab` is moved into the storage container of a `<KeepAlive>` that no longer exists:

- `isUnmounted` stays `false` and its effect scope stays active, so its watchers, intervals and other side effects keep running.
- `onUnmounted` / `onScopeDispose` never run, and nothing can unmount or reactivate it anymore.

Without step 2, or without the inner `<Suspense>`, `Tab` is unmounted as expected.

### System Info

```shell
  System:
    OS: Linux 6.17 Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS
    CPU: (14) x64 Intel(R) Core(TM) Ultra 7 265U
    Memory: 18.33 GB / 61.23 GB
  Binaries:
    Node: 24.15.0
    npm: 11.12.1
    pnpm: 12.10.1
  Browsers:
    Chrome: 155.0.8059.39
  npmPackages:
    vue: 3.5.44
    nuxt: 4.6.1 (original app)
    vue-router: 5.4.0 (original app)
```

### Any additional comments?

**Where we hit it.** This is the tree Nuxt renders for a page with `<NuxtPage keepalive>`, where each page is wrapped in a `<Suspense>` inside the root boundary. Navigating from such a page to a page with an async setup changes the route, so the old page's `<NuxtPage>` re-renders while the root boundary is pending. The visible child route then leaks on every such navigation. In our app the leaked tabs kept polling the API every 10 s after the user had left the page.

**Cause**, as far as I could trace it:

1. On the re-render, the inner `<Suspense>` is patched while an ancestor boundary is pending, so `SuspenseImpl.process` takes its early return (`parentSuspense.deps > 0`). It adopts the new vnode as `suspense.vnode` but never patches it, so `suspense.activeBranch` is still the vnode that is actually mounted.
2. `KeepAlive`'s `instance.subTree` now points to the new Suspense vnode, whose `ssContent` was never mounted.
3. When the root boundary resolves and `Shell` unmounts, `KeepAlive`'s `onBeforeUnmount` finds the current entry (`cached.type === vnode.type && cached.key === vnode.key`) and calls `resetShapeFlag(vnode)` with `vnode = getInnerChild(subTree)`. That is the never-mounted `ssContent`, not the mounted `activeBranch`.
4. The mounted vnode keeps `COMPONENT_SHOULD_KEEP_ALIVE`, so unmounting the inner `<Suspense>` calls `deactivate` on it instead of unmounting it. The first `Tab deactivated` is the `da` hook that `onBeforeUnmount` queues, the second one is this `deactivate`.

At `onBeforeUnmount` time in the reproduction, `subTree.ssContent !== subTree.suspense.activeBranch`: the first one has both keep-alive flags (768, it went through the cached path), the mounted one only `COMPONENT_SHOULD_KEEP_ALIVE` (256).

**Since when.** Bisected with the same reproduction: 3.4.8 and earlier unmount `Tab`. From 3.4.9 to 3.4.19 the root boundary never resolves in this scenario. From 3.4.20 on, `Tab` leaks as described. That lines up with the early return added in #10055 (3.4.9) and changed in #10184 (3.4.20).

**Related.** #15288 (the same early return, with KeepAlive caching a never-mounted vnode on a switch) and #15710 / #15711 (the same kind of flag reset on a vnode that is not the mounted one, in `pruneCacheEntry`). Neither covers the `onBeforeUnmount` path, and it still reproduces on 3.5.44.

**Possible fix.** In `onBeforeUnmount`, also reset the flag on the cached vnode, like #15711 does in `pruneCacheEntry`:

```js
if (cached.type === vnode.type && cached.key === vnode.key) {
  resetShapeFlag(vnode)
  resetShapeFlag(cached)
  // ...
}
```

I checked this by patching the 3.5.44 global build: `Tab` is then unmounted, also when the `<KeepAlive>` holds a second, non-visible child. Resetting `subTree.suspense.activeBranch` instead works too.

**Workaround** we use until then: a `router.beforeResolve` guard sets the KeepAlive's `include` to `[]` when the navigation leaves the page, so the cache is pruned while the tree is still mounted normally, before the root boundary goes pending.

I am happy to open a PR with the fix and a regression test.

title: KeepAlive + Suspense: async descendant resolving while inactive causes an infinite microtask retry loop on return

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the reported hang at the same root: the `pendingId` mismatch guard in `registerDep` no longer abandons an instance that is still alive (kept-alive or still in the active branch), so its setup/render actually completes instead of leaving `asyncResolved=false` for the renderer's async-root retry to spin on. All six independent tests pass on both, and each patch adds a repro test that fails on base.

The difference is in how they treat the issue's explicit constraint: 'keep the stale-branch guards and pending dependency counts correct for unrelated branches.' Patch A renders the stale instance immediately, even while the boundary is pending on a different tree. That render uses the same `suspense` as parent, so any async children the resolved component mounts call `registerDep` and increment `suspense.deps` under the *other* branch's `pendingId`. A slow or stuck descendant of the inactive cached page would then hold back the unrelated pending branch (e.g. navigating to an async page while the cached page's child finishes). A only patches around the symptom of this by splicing post-effects out of `suspense.effects`; it does not address the dep-count contamination. Its hydration branch simply reverts to base behaviour (abandon), which is not a regression but also not handled.

Patch B parks the stale instance's render in a `REQUEUE_ON_SUSPENSE_DISCARD` job until the boundary has no pending branch, re-parks it across discards, and explicitly excludes it from the dep count (`isPendingDep`). This keeps unrelated cycles' `deps` correct, which it verifies with the 'off-cycle async dep must not add its own async children to the pending cycle' test, plus cases for nested pending ancestors, out-in transitions, and hydration toggles. It also removes the `COMPONENT_KEPT_ALIVE` `pendingId` restoration, replacing that special case with the general stale-dep path; the `test.each` kept-alive scenarios cover what that line previously guaranteed, including that a discarded cycle is not counted down.

B is larger and touches the scheduler and three Suspense sites, which is real added risk, and I cannot confirm the existing suite still passes on either tree. But the extra machinery is targeted at a hole A leaves open and is backed by specific tests, whereas A's minimal change is cleaner but only partially honours the issue's stated requirement on unrelated branches. On correctness and test depth B is the better fix.

issue_md: ### Vue version 3.5.44; also reproduced with current `main` at `65eae178383289b6a9f93505ab85017460f72395`. ### Link to minimal reproduction [Open the single-file Vue Playground reproduction](https://play.vuejs.org/#) **Warning: clicking the button intentionally triggers an unresponsive preview.** The import map pins Vue's production runtime to **3.5.44**. No router, SSR, Nuxt, external requests, or application dependencies are required. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Open the reproduction and wait until the button is enabled. 2. The status should read: `Ready: the inner async child is still pending`. 3. Click **Run reproduction** once. 4. The preview becomes unresponsive; the success status never appears. The button performs this deterministic sequence, rather than relying on network timing: 1. Cache a page shell containing a still-pending async descendant. 2. Switch to another page and flush the update with `nextTick()`. 3. Resolve the descendant's loader **while its cached page is inactive**. 4. Wait for its Promise callbacks to run, using a macrotask boundary. 5. Return to the cached page and change the descendant's `revision` prop. The page shell uses a non-suspensible async wrapper to finish mounting first. Its inner async child retains the default `suspensible: true` behavior. ### What is expected? - Returning to the cached page displays `Async child loaded`. - The existing cached page remains usable, without an infinite update loop. - A retained child's async setup can finish, either while inactive or on reactivation. ### What is actually happening? - The loader Promise fulfills, but the retained instance stays `asyncResolved === false`. - Returning and updating its parent repeatedly retries an already-fulfilled Promise. - The resulting microtask loop prevents subsequent timers and UI work from running. This is an async retry loop, not a synchronous call-stack overflow. ### Complete App.vue Replace `App.vue` in a Vue SFC project with the following; no other files are needed. ```vue ``` ### State observations and preliminary diagnosis The following states were captured in a focused runtime-test fixture against current `main`. The async child remains mounted in a cached ancestor; it has not been unmounted. | Stage | Child `suspenseId` | Boundary `pendingId` | Child `asyncResolved` | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Inner async child starts loading | 0 | 0 | false | | Switch to the other page | 0 | 1 | false | | Loader fulfills while away | 0 | 1 | false | | Return and update the cached page | 0 | 0 | false | The last stage reaches `nextTick()`, but a subsequent timer never runs. An external watchdog terminated the isolated reproduction after three seconds. Relevant source, pinned to the tested commit: - [Suspense.registerDep](https://github.com/vuejs/core/blob/65eae178383289b6a9f93505ab85017460f72395/packages/runtime-core/src/components/Suspense.ts#L713-L786) - [Renderer async-root retry](https://github.com/vuejs/core/blob/65eae178383289b6a9f93505ab85017460f72395/packages/runtime-core/src/renderer.ts#L1433-L1452) The failure appears to cross these two paths: 1. Leaving switches the shared Suspense boundary to a different pending ID. 2. The cached page and its pending descendant are retained instead of unmounted. 3. When the loader fulfills, `registerDep()` rejects the mismatched pending ID. 4. It returns before `asyncResolved = true` and before `handleSetupResult()`. 5. Returning restores the old boundary ID, but the skipped Promise callback is not rerun. 6. The parent's component-root chain still contains that unresolved async instance. 7. `locateNonHydratedAsyncRoot()` finds it and schedules a retry after `asyncDep`. 8. That Promise has already fulfilled, so the retry immediately runs again. 9. The instance is still unresolved, so the same retry is scheduled indefinitely. Changing a fulfilled loader into a cached factory is not sufficient to finish this instance. The component definition has loaded; the retained instance's setup/render initialization has not. ### Controls and validation scope The following controls use the same SFC and Vue 3.5.44 production runtime: | Change | Result | | --- | --- | | Original sequence | Isolated process times out; success timer never runs | | Inner `AsyncChild` uses `suspensible: false` | Child renders; success timer runs | | Return before resolving the inner loader | Child renders; success timer runs | For the second control, change only the inner child's declaration: ```js const AsyncChild = defineAsyncComponent({ loader: () => childReady, suspensible: false, }) ``` For the third control, return and flush before calling `resolveChild()`. Tests performed: - The complete SFC above was compiled and mounted in jsdom 26.1.0 with Vue 3.5.44. - Its original sequence timed out; both controls completed and rendered the child. - A focused fixture against current `main` reproduced the state table and retry hang. - Earlier isolated production-runtime fixtures reproduced it on 3.5.22 and 3.6.0-rc.12. The RC test used the VDOM renderer, not Vapor. This is not a claim about all Vue versions. The SFC compiler used for the jsdom test was 3.5.22; the runtime under test was 3.5.44. No full repository test suite, build, or type check was run for this report. ### Possible fix direction — not a validated patch - Preserve or resume async initialization for descendants retained in a KeepAlive cache. - Distinguish a retained inactive branch from an abandoned/unmounted branch. - Prevent retries from looping when the awaited Promise is settled but setup is unresolved. - Keep the stale-branch guards and pending dependency counts correct for unrelated branches. Simply deleting the pending-ID guard could revive genuinely abandoned work. Simply setting `asyncResolved = true` would skip the missing setup/render initialization. Using separate cached, page-owned Suspense boundaries also passed an isolated 3.5.22 control. That is an application-level workaround, not a proposed or validated core patch. ### Related reports The navigation pattern resembles #6416 and #10899, but their fixes are already in tested versions. I am not claiming they are the same bug or that those fixes caused this issue. The distinguishing condition here is **loader completion while the retained page is inactive**. title: Suspense: reloading in quick succession with slow async `setup()` triggers HMR race

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the reported crash and the stale-render follow-up: the independent tests pass on A and B for both the nested-in-element and root-of-parent layouts, and both re-mark the instance dirty before calling parent.update() once the pending setup resolves, which is what the issue's analysis calls for.

B addresses the root cause more completely. The issue identifies the parent's postponement in componentUpdateFn via locateNonHydratedAsyncRoot as the reason the dirty mark goes stale. B reuses that exact function and loops: it waits on the instance's own asyncDep, then re-checks the parent's root chain and waits again if the freshly rendered instance exposed another pending async root (its nested test covers this). A only checks instance.asyncDep on the instance itself and then falls through to parent.update(); in the root-of-parent layout where the reloaded component's own root child is async and pending, A's parent.update() is postponed by the renderer, dirty.delete(instance) runs, and the child is patched rather than replaced, reproducing the 'keeps showing bar' symptom the issue describes. A's queueEffectWithSuspense trick only covers the case where the Suspense boundary itself is in a pending state, which is not the state these scenarios actually produce.

On edge handling the two trade blows: A's setupFailed fallthrough recovers after a rejected setup in the non-root layout without an errorHandler, while B silently drops the reload in that case (and both are stuck in the root layout). B's rejection test only covers the errorHandler path. A also adds a sensible adjacent guard in rerender() for a null job/update, which is useful but outside the issue's reload scenario and earns no credit by the rubric.

Tests: B's tests use explicit promise resolvers (deterministic) and cover both layouts, nested async roots, unmount during pending, and rejection; A's rely on wall-clock timeouts and cover both layouts, rejection, and rerender. One of B's test expectations on the versions array in the unmount test looks questionable, but the harness excludes patch-own test outcomes and I cannot verify it.

Craft: B guards with __FEATURE_SUSPENSE__ consistent with renderer.ts, uses try/finally to reset isHmrUpdating, and uses the scope.active check consistently; its only structural change is exporting locateNonHydratedAsyncRoot. A's design depends on Suspense effect-queue internals and a REQUEUE flag that rarely applies here.

Overall B's approach is the more principled and general fix of the mechanism the issue pinpoints, so B wins despite A's better behavior in one rejection edge case.

### Vue version

3.5.44, main

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

In the repro, click "Reload twice".

1. Show a page with a component whose <script setup> has a top-level await, e.g. await useFetch(...).
2. Save two modules that the component depends on within a few milliseconds of each other. For example, save two translation message file together, or use a formatter that writes several files. Vite then sends one update per file.

### What is expected?

The component is replaced, and shows the latest version without error.

### What is actually happening?

    TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'flags')
        at runtime-core.esm-bundler.js:568:28   (hmr.ts, the job queued in reload())
        at callWithErrorHandling
        at flushJobs

The page stops updating until it is reloaded.


### System Info

```shell
System:
    OS: Linux 7.0 Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS 26.04.1 LTS (Resolute Raccoon)
    CPU: (20) x64 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-13600
    Memory: 5.66 GB / 30.60 GB
    Container: Yes
    Shell: 5.3.9 - /bin/bash
  Binaries:
    Node: 22.23.3 - /snap/bin/node
    Yarn: 1.22.22 - /snap/bin/yarn
    npm: 10.9.9 - /snap/bin/npm
    pnpm: 8.15.9 - /home/tommie/node_modules/bin/pnpm
  Browsers:
    Chrome: 155.0.8059.79
```

### Any additional comments?

**Likely cause:**
- The first `reload()` remounts the instance.
- The new instance's `setup()` is async, so `mountComponent` registers it with the Suspense and defers `setupRenderEffect`. Until that runs, `instance.job` is `null`.
- The second `reload()` queues a job for that instance, and the job reads `instance.job.flags`. That check came from #13815, which assumes every instance has a job.

**Guarding the null is not enough:**
- With `instance.job ? !(instance.job.flags & DISPOSED) : !instance.isUnmounted`, the error goes away, but the child keeps showing `bar`.
- `instance.parent.update()` finds a pending async root (`locateNonHydratedAsyncRoot`) and postpones itself until `asyncDep` resolves.
- By then, the `queuePostFlushCb` at the end of `reload()` has cleared `hmrDirtyComponents`, so `isSameVNodeType` matches and the child is patched instead of replaced.
- The postponement is needed: the pending vnode has no `el`, so updating the parent at once fails in `hostParentNode(prevTree.el)`.

**Suggested fix:** in the queued job, wait for the pending setup to resolve, mark the instance dirty again, and then replace it.

title: compiler-dom: stringifyStatic renders :disabled="0" as a present attribute

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the same way: after evaluateConstant, every boolean attribute (and `hidden`) is dropped when includeBooleanAttr(evaluated) is false, and all independent tests pass on both. The difference is in craft, tests, and scope.

Patch B's core change is cleaner. It removes the now-redundant source-text `exp.content === 'false'` check and the odd `typeof` gating on `hidden`, leaving a single rule `(isBooleanAttr(arg) || arg === 'hidden') && !includeBooleanAttr(evaluated)` that matches the runtime/SSR rule the issue cites. Patch A keeps the old string check and adds a `typeof evaluated === 'number' || 'boolean'` clause for `hidden` that is dead weight (strings are either truthy or `''`, both kept by includeBooleanAttr; null is already filtered), so the resulting condition is harder to read than it needs to be.

Tests: Patch B covers a wider matrix of falsy constants (`0`, `-0`, `!1`, `1 > 2`, `0 / 0`, `null`, `void 0`) across disabled/checked/readonly/hidden, plus retained cases (`true`, `1`, `''`, `'false'`), plus a compiler+runtime integration test that mounts a stringified tree and asserts the button is enabled and clickable, which mirrors the issue's actual symptom. Patch A's tests are adequate (0 and !1 for three attrs, a truthy keep case, and `!1` added to the hidden test) but narrower.

Scope: Patch B goes beyond the ask by making analyzeNode bail on custom elements with boolean-attribute bindings and threading `context` through to do so. This is a behavior change (custom elements with `:disabled="true"` now deopt out of stringification) that the issue did not request, and it is the main mark against B. It is justified in a comment and covered by tests, and the signature change is contained to one call site, so the added risk is modest rather than disqualifying. Patch A is minimal and tightly scoped, which is its strongest point.

Weighing it: equal on correctness for the reported issue, B stronger on tests and on clarity of the core fix, A stronger on scope. The scope creep in B is defensible and tested, so B edges out overall.
